content: Specialist nursing roles are increasingly being utilized to manage stable disease populations, including bronchiectasis, as a response to the growing financial pressures on healthcare systems. Nurse-led care is being explored as an alternative to traditional doctor-led care, particularly in subacute, ambulatory, and community care settings. This review aimed to evaluate the safety, effectiveness, and health outcomes of nurses practicing autonomously with advanced skills in managing bronchiectasis. The objective of the review was to compare the effectiveness of nurse-led care versus doctor-led care in managing stable bronchiectasis. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted using the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register, bibliographies of selected papers, and grey literature, including clinical trial registries. The search was current as of March 2018. Only randomized controlled trials were eligible for inclusion in the review. Data extraction and analysis were performed by two reviewers. The primary outcomes assessed included the number of exacerbations requiring antibiotic treatment, hospital admissions, and emergency department visits. Secondary outcomes included healthcare resource utilization, treatment costs, quality of life, exercise capacity, mortality, and lung function. The review included a single randomized controlled trial conducted in the United Kingdom. This study involved 80 participants with a mean age of 58 years. Participants were treated by either a specialist nurse or a doctor for 12 months and then crossed over to the other clinician for the subsequent 12 months. Two participants died during the study, and six participants did not transition to nurse-led care due to unstable bronchiectasis. Overall, study completion rates were high. The data showed no significant difference in the number of exacerbations requiring antibiotic treatment between nurse-led and doctor-led care (rate ratio 1.09, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.91 to 1.30, moderate-certainty evidence). However, there were more hospital admissions in the nurse-led care group (rate ratio 1.52, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.23, moderate-certainty evidence). Emergency department attendance was not reported. Participants in the nurse-led care group utilized more healthcare resources during the first year of the trial, leading to higher treatment costs. Total costs for the two years of the study were £8,464 for nurse-led care compared to £5,228 for doctor-led care. However, by the second year, treatment costs between the two groups were nearly equivalent, possibly reflecting the nurses' improved ability to manage bronchiectasis over time. No statistically significant differences were observed in secondary outcomes, including quality of life, exercise capacity, mortality, or lung function. The wide confidence intervals for these outcomes introduced uncertainty into the findings. Adverse events were not assessed in this review. The authors concluded that only one trial met the inclusion criteria, and the evidence was insufficient to demonstrate the effectiveness of nurse-led care compared to doctor-led care. While the included study reported no significant differences in clinical outcomes, the limited evidence makes it unclear whether nurse-led care is as effective as doctor-led care in a specialist clinic setting. Further research is needed to determine the cost-effectiveness of nurse-led care, the impact of following bronchiectasis management guidelines on costs, and the effectiveness of nurse-led care in other clinical settings, such as inpatient and outreach care.
